SeriesLinearAlgAccessor::logdet¶

Back to SeriesLinearAlgAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

Series SeriesLinearAlgAccessor::logdet() const
Series SeriesLinearAlgProxy::logdet() const

What It Does¶

logdet() computes the real natural logarithm of each matrix determinant:

logdet(A) = log(det(A))

The real logarithm requires a positive determinant. A positive determinant produces a finite logarithm, a zero determinant produces negative infinity, and a negative determinant produces NaN because its logarithm is outside the real number domain.

Like det(), this method reduces the final two matrix dimensions and preserves all leading batch dimensions.

Why Work In Logarithmic Scale¶

Determinants multiply under matrix multiplication:

det(A B) = det(A) det(B)

Their logarithms therefore add whenever the determinants are positive:

logdet(A B) = logdet(A) + logdet(B)

This turns a potentially enormous or tiny multiplicative scale into a more manageable additive quantity. It also explains the domain: logdet() retains the ordinary real-logarithm meaning rather than discarding determinant sign. When sign is itself part of the result, slogdet() represents both sign and log-magnitude explicitly.

Shape Contract¶

Input shape

Output shape

One output value means

[n, n]

[]

log(det(A))

[b, n, n]

[b]

one log-determinant per batch member

[..., n, n]

[...]

one value per leading coordinate

The final two dimensions must be square. They are reduced; leading dimensions are not broadcast or combined.

Returns¶

Series A scalar or batch-shaped Series containing real log-determinants. Positive determinants produce their natural logarithm, zero determinants produce -inf, and negative determinants produce NaN.

Gradient¶

For an invertible matrix with positive determinant,

d log(det(A)) / dA = A^-T

With incoming sensitivity g, reverse mode returns g A^-T. This follows by dividing the determinant derivative det(A) A^-T by det(A): the potentially large determinant cancels, leaving the inverse transpose.

The derivative is not finite at a singular matrix, and a negative determinant lies outside this method’s real-valued forward domain.

Examples¶

Example 1. Compute the logarithm of a positive determinant.

auto matrix = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 7.0}, {2.0, 6.0}});
std::cout << matrix.linearalg.logdet() << "\n";

The determinant is 10, so the result is log(10).

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=2.3025851

Example 2. Determinant sign controls the real logarithm’s result.

auto positive = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 7.0}, {2.0, 6.0}});
auto negative = pluss::make_series({{2.0, 6.0}, {4.0, 7.0}});
auto singular = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {2.0, 4.0}});

std::cout << "positive=" << positive.linearalg.logdet() << "\n";
std::cout << "negative=" << negative.linearalg.logdet() << "\n";
std::cout << "singular=" << singular.linearalg.logdet() << "\n";

The second matrix has determinant -10, while the third has determinant zero.

Output¶

positive=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=2.3025851
negative=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=nan
singular=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=-inf

Example 3. A batch preserves one output dimension for its three matrices.

auto batch = pluss::make_series({
    {{1.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 3.0}},
    {{2.0, 1.0}, {1.0, 2.0}},
    {{1.0, 2.0}, {2.0, 4.0}},
});

std::cout << batch.linearalg.logdet() << "\n";

The first two determinants are 3; the final matrix is singular.

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0986123, 1.0986123, -inf]

Example 4. The reverse sensitivity is the inverse transpose.

auto matrix = pluss::make_series({{2.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 4.0}});
matrix.tracks_slope_(true);

matrix.linearalg.logdet().reverse();

std::cout << matrix.sensitivity() << "\n";

The matrix is diagonal, so its inverse transpose is diag(1/2, 1/4).

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.5, 0],
  [-0, 0.25]]

Example 5. The additive rule can replace a product determinant calculation when both determinants are positive.

auto a = pluss::make_series({{2.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 3.0}});
auto b = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 5.0}});

std::cout << "product=" << a.linearalg.mm(b).linearalg.logdet() << "\n";
std::cout << "sum=" << a.linearalg.logdet().add(b.linearalg.logdet()) << "\n";

Both expressions equal log(120).

Output¶

product=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=4.7874917
sum=pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[4.7874917]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • logdet() means log(det(A)), not log(abs(det(A))).

  • Negative determinants produce NaN; use slogdet() when the sign and logarithm of the magnitude are both meaningful to the algorithm.

  • Singular matrices produce -inf, and their derivative is not finite.

  • Input must end in two equal matrix dimensions.

Summary¶

logdet() maps each positive determinant into the real logarithmic domain, turning multiplicative matrix scale into an additive quantity. Its output has the batch shape, and its gradient is the inverse transpose.
